title: Autoremediation cookbook: Terraform guards, healthcheck sagas, and private deployment recovery
creator: Aisha Chen
description:
Summary:
This ticket captures an operationally-focused, implementation-ready runbook and set of automated remediation sagas for common Private (VPC) health-check failures. Goal: reduce mean-time-to-recover for regularly observed failure classes to under 5 minutes for low-severity incidents and enable safe automated remediation for medium-severity incidents with human-in-the-loop approvals when risk is elevated. This includes Terraform/IaC drift detection and safe auto-fix guards, ephemeral instance recovery, network sanity checks, and module-based upgrade canaries.

Motivation and scope:
- Operators frequently triage three recurring classes of incidents in Private: (A) agent processes or inference nodes becoming unreachable (network or host-level), (B) Terraform/IaC drift or configuration mismatch after upgrades, and (C) degraded kernel scheduling or queue buildups leading to SLO breaches.
- We will deliver: (1) a prescriptive runbook for each class, (2) idempotent remediation sagas implemented as step functions / workflows, (3) Terraform module patterns and guard rails (plan-time checks, selective auto-apply), and (4) alerting and dashboards to validate remediation effectiveness.

Runbook: Failure class A — Node unreachable / agent offline (common causes: OS crash, docker/agent oom, route/security-group change, host terminated)
1) Detection:
   - Alert triggers: vpc.agent_unreachable_count > 0 for 2m OR grpc-ping failures to node > 3 in 30s.
   - Key dashboards: vpc-healthcheck-overview, agent-heartbeats by region.
2) Automated saga (safe default):
   - Step 1: Orchestrator posts a Slack alert to #private-ops with automated remediation candidate and a 90s hold timer.
   - Step 2: Run quick probing script (via SSM or exec in control plane) to collect: systemd status, docker ps, kernel logs, route tables, security group diff.
   - Step 3: If probes indicate process OOM or docker restartable error, issue a targeted agent container restart (docker restart <agent>) and re-check health.
   - Step 4: If host is unresponsive to SSM, attempt soft reboot via cloud provider API (with idempotency tokens).
   - Step 5: If still down after 3 attempts or host marked unhealthy by cloud provider, spin a replacement from the same launch template, attach to same subnets, and gracefully cordon+drain failed node via orchestration.
   - Safety guard: if > 30% of pool is unhealthy, abort automated replacement and escalate to on-call.
3) Manual steps / escalation: collect core dumps, open support tickets with cloud vendor, and notify affected customers if SLOs are impacted.

Runbook: Failure class B — IaC drift or Terraform plan failures after upgrade (common causes: manually-touched SGs/route tables, drift in AMI IDs, module version incompatibility)
1) Detection:
   - Daily sentinel job runs: terraform plan in a read-only fashion for all Private module stacks. Any non-empty diff creates an incident.
   - Alerts for plan-failures during automated upgrades (upgrade pipeline runs terraform plan -> apply).
2) Automated saga (remediation candidate):
   - Step 1: Classify diff via heuristic rules: benign tag/metadata-only vs security-group/route/iam changes.
   - Step 2: For metadata-only changes and tag drift, auto-apply via a controlled terraform apply with a changelog and commit to infra-repo.
   - Step 3: For network/iam changes, create a draft PR and notify infra-owners; block auto-apply.
   - Step 4: If drift indicates missing resources (e.g., detached SG rule preventing healthchecks), attempt a targeted patch (terraform apply -target=module.vpc.aws_security_group.rule_healthcheck) with a pre-approved guardrail list.
   - Safety guard: all auto-applies require the plan to be < 5 resources changed and not modify IAM or IAM policies. Otherwise require human approval.
3) Upgrade staging canary pattern:
   - Any Terraform module upgrade must be run through a canary workspace that targets a single small VPC stack. Health checks and load tests run for 30m. If stable, promotion to batch apply across other stacks with progressive rollout.

Runbook: Failure class C — Scheduling/backlog and slow kernel selection (manifesting as increased P95 latency and token throughput drops)
1) Detection:
   - Alerts when p95 latency > threshold AND queue depth for a model shard > X for 5m.
   - Instrumentation: per-shard queue depth, batch sizes, CPU/GPU saturation metrics, kernel fallback counts.
2) Automated mitigation steps:
   - Step 1: If batch sizes are below expected and queue depth high, trigger ephemeral scaling policy to increase worker count by 10% (up to burst cap).
   - Step 2: If kernel fallback is detected (e.g., non-optimized kernel in use), trigger a staged process to swap to the prebuilt binary optimized kernel. This uses the runtime runtime-switcher service which performs a rolling restart per node.
   - Step 3: If scheduling backlog persists after 3 scaling waves, switch traffic away from the affected model variant to a compatible lower-latency variant (via smart routing policy) with automatic throttling.
   - Safety guard: traffic shifting limited to 25% per minute and requires integration test verification for structured-output compatibility.

Terraform / IaC patterns and guard rails included in deliverable:
- Module layout: separate modules for network (vpc, subnets, sg), compute (autoscaling groups / instance profiles), runtime config (agent ASG launch templates, AMI IDs, container args).
- Sentinel checks (or terraform-cloud policies): prevent auto-apply of IAM changes and block downgrades of AMI unless explicit flag set.
- Drift sentinel: daily plan -> structured diff -> classification -> remediation pipeline.
- Idempotent apply patterns: use -target scoped applies only from a safe allowlist; require PR + changelog for cross-cutting changes.

Observability & verification:
- Post-remediation probes: run the standard healthcheck suite (network, grpc/echo, KV reconciliation) and verify token-level latency against baseline for 15m before closing incident automatically.
- Dashboard panels to show remediation success rate, MTTR trend, and false-positive auto-applies.
- Audit logs: every automated action must produce a signed event (user=system:autoremediation, reason, plan hash) stored in the control-plane audit store.

Testing plan and staged rollout:
- Unit tests for each saga step (mocks for SSM, cloud API, terraform plan).
- Integration tests in a sandbox VPC using test harness that injects failure modes (OOM, route deletion, drift).
- Initial rollout: enable automatic remediation with conservative guards in 1 region and observe for 2 weeks, then expand.

Operational notes and runbook consumption:
- This ticket contains the canonical runbook content and the initial implementation for the automation sagas. A confluence runbook will be created and linked (see attachments).
- On-call flow: automated remediation posts to #private-ops; if the saga escalates, the on-call receives a call and should follow the manual checklist included below.

Manual checklist (short):
- Collect logs: journalctl -u redwood-agent, docker logs --since 1h <agent>, dmesg.
- Check infra: aws ec2 describe-instance-status, aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-instances, cloud provider health events.
- Terraform: run terraform plan, capture diff, and tag incident with plan-hash.
- If performing a replacement, ensure new instance includes same launch-template metadata and custom user-data markers.

Acceptance criteria:
- A set of automated sagas for the three failure classes implemented in step-functions/workflow engine and deployed behind feature flags.
- Terraform sentinel rules and canary workspace flow implemented and documented.
- Post-remediation verification circuit and dashboards are live.
- On-call runbook published in Confluence and referenced in #private-ops.
- Automated tests covering the main success/failure paths.

Open implementation tasks (short):
- Implement the probing agent that runs pre-remediation diagnostics (PR: infra#4321).
- Wire up the SSM-based container restart action and idempotent reboot step.
- Add terraform plan classifier rules to infra pipeline and implement targeted apply allowlist.
- Create canary workspace and deploy to staging VPC.

Notes / design trade-offs:
- We explicitly avoid broad automatic IAM changes or large-scale terraform auto-applies because the blast radius is high; for those we favor PR generation and human review.
- Replacements are cheapest and fastest for single-node failures, but harmful under correlated failures; hence the 30% pool guard.
- Traffic shifting should prefer model-variant fallback rather than global rollback to avoid service-wide regression.

Contacts and owners:
- Ownership: Platform Infra (Marco Alvarez), Runtime Reliability (Priya Natarajan).
- Escalation: On-call rotation (see internal roster).

Terraform sentinel rules enforce guard rails; canary workspace functional
